MEDI2200 · Week 3 · Cell Division — Dr Lucinda McRobb

Cell division — packaging the genome & mitosis

Two questions, one week: how do two metres of DNA fold into a nucleus, and how is that genome copied and split perfectly into two cells? This guide merges both Week-3 modules — DNA organisation (chromatin → chromosome → the human karyotype) and the mitotic cell cycle. Part 1 is built from the module's own figures.

Covers 2 modules · 5 LOs Figures 8 plates from your module Recall 6 section checklists

§0DNA organisation · LO1

Packaging the genome

Two metres of DNA, folded to fit — and folded so it can still be read.

Eukaryotes keep their DNA in a membrane-bound nucleus; prokaryotes have none, their DNA sitting free as a folded nucleoid (Plate 0.1). Eukaryotes also carry far more DNA — the human genome stretched out is about 2 metres long, yet it fits inside a nucleus a few microns across. That demands serial folding.

Label Key — two cell plans
Eukaryote
DNA enclosed in a nucleus (bounded by the nuclear membrane); also has membrane organelles (e.g. mitochondria). Far more DNA.
Prokaryote
No nucleus — the single chromosome is a folded nucleoid free in the cytoplasm.

The levels of packing

Various enzymes and proteins condense the DNA in stages. The double-stranded DNA is first wound around a series of proteins called histones; DNA + histones together form nucleosomes — the basic repeating unit of the condensed DNA, which is termed chromatin.

Further looping and supercoiling of chromatin during cell division produces the tight, familiar chromosome. Plate 0.2 is the whole ladder in one image.

Label Key — climbing the ladder
DNA double helix
The bare sequence — far too long to fit unpacked.
DNA wrapped around histone
The DNA winds around histone cores, forming nucleosomes ("beads on a string").
Nucleosomes coiled into a chromatin fibre
The beaded string coils into the ~30 nm chromatin fibre.
Further condensation
The fibre loops and supercoils onto a protein scaffold.
Duplicated chromosome
Maximal condensation — the compact chromosome seen at cell division.
🤔 Predict · before you read on

Packing lets 2 m of DNA fit inside a micron-wide nucleus. Beyond simply fitting, what two other problems does condensing the genome solve?

It makes the genome manageable to segregate — an unpacked thread would tangle and snap when hauled apart at division — and it regulates genes, because DNA wound too tight to be read is effectively switched off. One mechanism, three payoffs: it fits, it divides cleanly, it regulates.
Reasoning · packing solves two problems at once

Condensing DNA isn't only about fit. A 2-metre thread crammed into a nucleus would tangle and break when pulled apart at division — so packing also makes the genome manageable to segregate. And because a gene buried in tightly-wound chromatin can't be reached by the reading machinery, how tightly a region is packed also decides whether its genes are switched on (§1). One mechanism, three payoffs: it fits, it divides cleanly, and it regulates.

Memory hook · the packing ladder

DNA → Nucleosomes → Chromatin → Chromosome — "Dogs Need Chew Chews." Beads-on-a-string (nucleosomes) is the rung everyone forgets.

R Recall checklist — packaging
  • Eukaryote = DNA in a nucleus; prokaryote = free nucleoid, no nucleus.
  • ~2 m of DNA must fit into a micron-scale nucleus.
  • Packing ladder — DNA → (histones) nucleosomes → chromatin fibre → condensed chromosome.
  • Nucleosome = DNA wound on histones; the repeating unit of chromatin.
§1Chromatin · LO1

Chromatin: euchromatin vs heterochromatin

How tightly a region is wound decides whether its genes can be read.

In a non-dividing cell, chromatin exists in two states you can literally see on an electron micrograph (Plate 1.1): pale, open regions and dark, dense regions.

Label Key — reading the EM
Euchromatin (light)
Loosely packed, gene-rich and active — open enough for the transcription machinery to reach the DNA.
Heterochromatin (dark)
Tightly packed and transcriptionally inactive — the DNA is inaccessible.
The two chromatin states
EuchromatinHeterochromatin
PackingLoose / openTight / condensed
On EMLightDark
Gene activityActive (accessible)Silent (inaccessible)
Opened / closed byHATs (acetylation) → openHDACs, KMTs, DNMTs (deacetylation/methylation) → closed

Heterochromatin itself comes in two kinds: constitutive heterochromatin is always condensed (the structural regions — centromeres and telomeres), while facultative heterochromatin is condensed only in certain cells or at certain times — classically an entire inactivated X chromosome during development.

🤔 Predict · before you read on

Every cell in your body carries the same DNA sequence, yet a neuron behaves nothing like a liver cell. What decides which genes run — without altering a single base?

How tightly each region is wound. Open (acetylated) chromatin is readable and its genes are active; densely packed chromatin is silenced. Enzymes tune the winding cell-by-cell, so one identical genome can run a neuron or a liver cell — the basis of epigenetics.
Reasoning · packing = an on/off switch for genes

The degree of winding is a gene switch that never touches the DNA sequence — the basis of epigenetics. Enzymes tune it: histone acetyltransferases (HATs) loosen the grip of histones on DNA, opening chromatin for active transcription; HDACs (deacetylation), histone methyltransferases (KMTs) and DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) tighten it, giving repressed transcription. Because this is reversible and doesn't alter the code, the same genome can run a neuron and a liver cell.

Clinical / real-world · epigenetics in disease

Getting these marks wrong causes disease. Many cancers epigenetically silence tumour-suppressor genes by hyper-methylating their promoters (DNMTs) — the gene is intact but locked in heterochromatin. This is druggable: DNMT and HDAC inhibitors are used in some blood cancers to re-open wrongly-silenced genes. X-inactivation (facultative heterochromatin) is why females are mosaics for X-linked traits.

Memory hook · which is active

EUchromatin = "you can use it" (open, expressed). HETEROchromatin = "hidden" (dense, silent). Acetylation Activates.

R Recall checklist — chromatin
  • Euchromatin — loose, light, gene-rich, active.
  • Heterochromatin — tight, dark, inactive; constitutive (centromere/telomere) vs facultative (X-inactivation).
  • Epigenetic control — HATs open (acetylation → active); HDACs/KMTs/DNMTs close (→ repressed).
  • Sequence unchanged — packing, not mutation, sets expression.
§2Chromosome structure · LO2

Chromosome structure

Two arms, a centromere, two caps — every feature earns its place at division.

Prior to division, each chromosome's DNA replicates, producing two identical copies held together until anaphase and termed sister chromatids. Plate 2.1 names the parts of the familiar duplicated (X-shaped) chromosome.

Label Key — the parts
Chromatid
One of the two identical DNA copies; together the pair are sister chromatids.
Centromere
The constriction joining the sister chromatids and the spindle-attachment point — the key to accurate segregation.
Short arm (p) / Long arm (q)
The two arms either side of the centromere — p = "petit" (short), q = "queue" (long).
Telomere
The protective cap on each chromosome end (§2.1).

The centromere can lie anywhere along the chromosome, and its position classifies the chromosome — Plate 2.2: metacentric (central), submetacentric (off-centre), acrocentric (near one end) and telocentric (at the very end — not found in humans, but common in mice).

Label Key — from end to centre
Telocentric
Centromere right at the end (no short arm) — not in humans.
Acrocentric
Centromere near one end — a tiny p-arm.
Metacentric
Centromere central — arms roughly equal.
Submetacentric
Centromere off-centre — unequal arms.
🤔 Predict · before you read on

A chromosome loses its centromere. Predict what happens to it at the next cell division.

It's lost. The centromere is where the spindle grabs the chromosome (via the kinetochore) to drag sister chromatids to opposite poles — no centromere, no attachment, so the chromosome can't be segregated and the daughter cells end up with the wrong chromosome count.
Reasoning · why the centromere is non-negotiable

The centromere is where the spindle grabs the chromosome (via the kinetochore) to haul the sister chromatids to opposite poles. Lose or mis-place it and the chromosome can't be segregated — daughters end up with the wrong number of chromosomes. That's why a "chromosome" without a functional centromere is lost at the next division: every structural feature here exists to make accurate distribution at mitosis possible.

Memory hook · the arms

p = petit = short arm (on top); q = queue = long arm (below). "p before q, short before long."

§2.1Telomeres, senescence & telomerase

Telomeres are repetitive DNA structures capping each chromosome end. The repeats form a loop that recruits protective proteins (Plate 2.3), and they do three protective jobs: stop chromosome ends fusing (end-joining), protect the ends from nuclease digestion, and stop the DNA-repair machinery mistaking the natural end for a double-strand break. They are also essential for replicating the very end of the DNA.

Label Key — the cap
Telomere repeats
Non-coding repeats at each end — a buffer that can be lost without losing genes.
The loop
The repeats fold into a loop that recruits protective proteins, hiding the end.

But there's a cost. Because DNA polymerase can't fully copy the very end of a linear chromosome (the end-replication problem), telomeres shorten a little with each division.

When they get critically short the cell stops dividing — replicative senescence — and the number of divisions a normal cell can make is the Hayflick limit.

The enzyme telomerase re-adds telomeric repeats, resetting the clock; it's active in stem and germ cells.

🤔 Predict · before you read on

DNA polymerase can't copy the very end of a linear chromosome. Given that, what must happen to the telomere with every division — and where does it eventually lead?

Telomeres shorten a little each division (the end-replication problem). When they get critically short the cell stops dividing — replicative senescence, capped by the Hayflick limit. The enzyme telomerase can re-add the repeats and reset the clock — which most cancers hijack to divide without limit.
Clinical / real-world · telomeres, ageing & cancer

Telomeres are a double-edged clock. Their shortening limits how long tissues can renew — senescent cells accumulate as we age (and are normally cleared by the immune system; premature-ageing disorders like Werner syndrome involve this machinery). But the same clock is a tumour-suppressor: it caps how many times a cell can divide. Most cancers escape it by reactivating telomerase, gaining unlimited divisions — which is exactly why telomerase is a target of interest in oncology.

Memory hook · the caps

Telomeres = the plastic tips on shoelaces — they stop the ends fraying (fusing/digesting). They wear down each division; telomerase re-tips them (stem, germ & cancer cells).

R Recall checklist — chromosome structure
  • Sister chromatids — 2 identical copies joined at the centromere until anaphase.
  • Arms — p (petit/short) & q (queue/long); centromere = spindle attachment.
  • Classification — metacentric / submetacentric / acrocentric / telocentric (not human).
  • Telomeres — caps that prevent fusion, nuclease digestion & false DSB signalling.
  • Shorten each division → senescence (Hayflick); telomerase re-extends (stem/germ/cancer).
§3Human genome · LO3

The human genome & nomenclature

46 chromosomes, 23 pairs — and an address system for every gene.

The human genome is 46 chromosomes = 23 pairs (Plate 3.1). The two members of a pair are homologous chromosomes — one inherited from each parent, carrying the same genes (though possibly different alleles). Twenty-two pairs are autosomes; the last pair are the sex chromosomes (XX female, XY male).

Label Key — reading a karyotype
Pairs 1–22
The autosomes, arranged in roughly decreasing size — each a matched homologous pair.
X / Y
The sex chromosomes — XX (female) or XY (male).
The whole layout
A karyogram — chromosomes isolated when highly condensed and arranged to check number and structure.

Staining gives each chromosome a striped banding pattern — a unique signature used to identify it and to spot structural abnormalities.

Bands give every gene an address (Plate 3.2): a chromosomal locus is written as chromosome number + arm (p or q) + region + band + sub-band. So 3p22.1 means chromosome 3, short (p) arm, region 2, band 2, sub-band 1 — and bands are numbered outward from the centromere.

Label Key — building the address
p-arm ("petit") / q-arm ("queue")
Short and long arms — the first letter of the address.
ptel / qtel
The p and q telomeres — the arm ends.
Region · band · sub-band
Numbered outward from the centromere: 3p 2(region) 2(band) .1(sub-band) = 3p22.1.
Reasoning · why banding makes genetics visible

The karyotype is how you see a genome. Condensing the chromosomes makes them individually distinguishable; ordering them by size and giving each a reproducible banding signature turns an otherwise invisible molecular event — an extra chromosome, a deleted arm, a swapped segment — into something you can count and locate by eye. The locus address (3p22.1) is the shared coordinate system that lets clinicians and researchers point to exactly the same spot.

Clinical / real-world · why the karyotype matters

Karyotyping and banding are front-line clinical genetics. Counting reveals aneuploidy — an extra chromosome 21 (three copies) is trisomy 21 / Down syndrome; missing or extra sex chromosomes give Turner (45,X) or Klinefelter (47,XXY). Banding reveals structural changes — a swapped segment between chromosomes 9 and 22 (the Philadelphia chromosome) drives chronic myeloid leukaemia. The locus address (e.g. 3p22.1) is how such changes are pinpointed and communicated.

Memory hook · 46, 23, 22+1

46 chromosomes = 23 pairs = 22 autosome pairs + 1 sex pair. Locus reads outside-in from the centromere: chr → arm → region → band → sub-band.

R Recall checklist — the genome
  • 46 chromosomes = 23 pairs; homologous pairs (one per parent).
  • 22 autosome pairs + 1 sex pair (XX / XY).
  • Karyotype/karyogram — arrange by size to check number & structure.
  • Locus = chr + arm(p/q) + region + band + sub-band (e.g. 3p22.1); bands count out from the centromere.
§4Cell division · LO4

Why cells divide

Two goals — copy the genome exactly, or reshuffle it on purpose.

Cell division serves two very different ends, and the human body uses two processes to match. Somatic (body) cells divide by mitosis — for growth in the embryo and child, for everyday tissue maintenance, and for repair — producing genetically identical diploid daughters (genomic stability). Germ cells (ovaries, testes) divide by meiosis to make haploid gametes for sexual reproduction, deliberately generating genetic variation.

Mitosis vs meiosis — matching the job to the process
MitosisMeiosis
WhereSomatic (body) cellsGerm cells (ovaries, testes)
PurposeGrowth, maintenance, repairProduce gametes for reproduction
Daughters2, diploid, identical4, haploid, genetically varied
GenomeConserved exactly (stability)Reshuffled (variation)

Prokaryotes take a much simpler route — binary fission: the single chromosome is replicated, the two copies segregate to opposite ends, and the cell splits into two identical daughters. It's fast and gives exponential growth, but with none of the checkpoints and machinery a mammalian cell needs.

Reasoning · stability vs variation, by design

The contrast is the whole point. A liver that repaired itself with varied cells would be chaos, so somatic division (mitosis) copies the genome exactly. But a species whose offspring were all identical couldn't adapt, so reproductive division (meiosis) shuffles the genome. Same cell, opposite requirements — which is why the mitotic machinery of §5 is built around fidelity and control.

R Recall checklist — why divide
  • Somatic → mitosis — growth/maintenance/repair; identical diploid daughters (stability).
  • Germ → meiosis — haploid gametes; genetic variation.
  • Prokaryotes → binary fission — replicate, segregate, split; exponential growth.
§5Mitotic cell cycle · LO5

The mitotic cell cycle & mitosis

Grow, copy, check, split — and check again at every gate.

Note: this second module was delivered as lecture recordings, so the detail below follows the module's stated learning objectives and standard cell biology rather than its own slides — cross-check the emphasis against your lecture videos. (No figures are invented for this part.)

The cell cycle: interphase + M phase

A dividing cell runs a cycle with two big parts. Most of the time is spent in interphase, which has three stages, followed by the brief M phase where division actually happens. Cells that aren't dividing rest in a quiescent state, G0.

Stages of the cell cycle
PhaseWhat happens
G1 (interphase)Cell grows, makes proteins/organelles, and checks it's ready to commit to division.
S (interphase)DNA is replicated — each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids.
G2 (interphase)Further growth; checks DNA is fully and correctly copied before dividing.
M (mitotic phase)Mitosis (nuclear division) + cytokinesis (cytoplasmic division).
G0Quiescent — a resting state outside the cycle (many mature cells sit here).

M phase: the stages of mitosis

Mitosis divides the replicated nucleus into two identical nuclei, in four classic stages, after which cytokinesis splits the cell:

Mitosis, stage by stage
StageKey event
ProphaseChromatin condenses into visible chromosomes (each = 2 sister chromatids); the mitotic spindle forms and the nuclear envelope breaks down.
MetaphaseSpindle fibres align the chromosomes along the middle — the metaphase plate.
AnaphaseThe centromeres split and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles.
TelophaseA nuclear envelope re-forms around each set; chromosomes decondense.
CytokinesisThe cytoplasm divides, giving two genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
Memory hook · the order of mitosis

Prophase → Metaphase → Anaphase → Telophase = "PMAT." Metaphase = Middle; Anaphase = Apart.

§5.1Principles of cell-cycle progression

Progression through the cycle is driven by cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), and policed at checkpoints that halt the cycle until conditions are right:

The cell-cycle checkpoints
CheckpointAsks before allowing progression
G1/S (restriction point)Is the cell big enough, are nutrients/growth signals present, and is the DNA undamaged?
G2/MHas all the DNA been replicated correctly and is it undamaged?
Spindle (M) checkpointIs every chromosome correctly attached to the spindle before the chromatids are pulled apart?
Reasoning · checkpoints protect the genome

Each checkpoint is a "don't proceed until…" gate. They exist because the payoff of §4 — identical daughters — fails if a cell divides with half-copied, damaged, or mis-attached chromosomes. Cyclin/CDK activity is the accelerator; the checkpoints are the brakes that make sure the accelerator only fires when it's safe.

🤔 Predict · before you read on

Cyclins and CDKs are the accelerator of the cell cycle; the checkpoints (like p53) are the brakes. Predict what a cell starts doing if the brakes fail.

It divides with damaged or half-copied DNA — accumulating mutations and proliferating unchecked. That is cancer at its core: oncogenes jam the accelerator, and lost tumour-suppressors (p53) release the brakes. It's also why many chemotherapies strike the cell cycle directly.
Clinical / real-world · when control fails — cancer

Cancer is, at its core, a disease of this control system. Mutations that jam the accelerator (oncogenes) or disable the brakes (tumour-suppressors like p53, the "guardian" that enforces the DNA-damage checkpoints) let cells divide with damaged genomes — accumulating more mutations and dividing uncontrollably. It's also why many chemotherapies target the cell cycle — hitting rapidly dividing cells at S phase or the spindle (M phase).

R Recall checklist — the mitotic cell cycle
  • Cycle = interphase (G1 grow · S replicate · G2 prep) + M (mitosis + cytokinesis); G0 = resting.
  • Mitosis = PMAT — Prophase (condense/spindle/envelope breaks) → Metaphase (align) → Anaphase (chromatids apart) → Telophase (re-form nuclei) → cytokinesis.
  • Result — 2 identical diploid daughter cells.
  • Drive vs brakes — cyclins/CDKs drive; checkpoints (G1/S, G2/M, spindle) verify.
  • Checkpoint failure → uncontrolled division (cancer; p53 = guardian).
